chunks: Al-Muzaffar ibn Ja'far (ibn al-Muzaffar) ibn al-Alawi al-Samarqandi (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us; Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Mas'ud al-Ayashi, from his father, who said: Abdullah ibn Muhammad Khalid al-Tayalesi narrated to us, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-Azdi, from Hamzah ibn Humran, from his father Humran ibn A'yn, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali al-Baqir (peace be upon them both).

He said: Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) used to pray one thousand units of prayer in the day and night, as the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to do. He had five hundred date palms, and he would pray two units of prayer at each palm tree. When he stood in his prayer, his color changed to another color. His standing in prayer was like the standing of a humble servant before the Majestic King. His limbs trembled from the fear of Allah, the Exalted. He prayed a prayer of farewell, considering that he would never pray after it again. One day, while he was praying, his cloak slipped off one of his shoulders, and he did not adjust it until he finished his prayer. Some of his companions asked him about that, and he said: 'Woe to you! Do you know before whom you are standing? Indeed, Allah accepts from a servant's prayer only that portion for which he directed his heart with full attention.' The man said: 'We are ruined!' He said: 'No, indeed Allah, the Exalted, will perfect that with the voluntary prayers (Nawafil).'

He (peace be upon him) would go out in the dark of the night carrying a bag on his back containing bundles of dinars and dirhams. Sometimes he would carry food or firewood on his back until he went door to door, knocked, and handed it to whoever came out. He would cover his face when giving to a poor person so that they would not recognize him. When he passed away, they missed that sign and realized it was Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him). When he was placed on the washing sheet, they looked at his back and saw it was rough like a camel's knee from carrying loads on his back to the homes of the poor and the needy.

One day he went out wearing a fur cloak. A beggar came and clung to the cloak; he left it and walked away. He would buy fur in winter, and when summer came, he would sell it and give the money in charity. On the Day of Arafat, he saw a group of people asking others for things, and he said to them: 'Woe to you! Do you ask people other than Allah on such a day? Indeed, hope is placed on this day for those in the wombs of pregnant women that they may be fortunate.'

He (peace be upon him) would abstain from eating food with his mother. It was said to him: 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, you are the most dutiful to kin and the best at maintaining family ties; why do you not eat with your mother?' He said: 'I dislike for my hand to reach out to what her eyes have already seen.' A man said to him: 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, I love you for Allah with a strong love.' He replied: 'O Allah, I seek refuge in You that I love for Your sake while You hate me.'

He performed Hajj twenty times riding his own camel, never striking it with a whip. When she died, he ordered her to be buried so that beasts would not eat her. A female slave of his was asked about him; she was told to be concise. She said: 'I never brought him food during the day, nor did I spread out his bed for him at night.'

One day he came upon a group of people who were backbiting him. He stood before them and said: 'If you are truthful, may Allah forgive me; if you are lying, may Allah forgive you.' When a seeker of knowledge came to him, he would say: 'Welcome to the Messenger's deputy (peace be upon him and his family).' Then he would say: 'Indeed, when a seeker of knowledge leaves his house, he does not place his feet on wet or dry ground except that glorification is said for him up to the seventh earth.'

He used to support one hundred poor families in Medina. He liked for orphans, the helpless, the weak, and the destitute to sit at his table. He would feed them with his own hand, and for those who had dependents, he would carry food for their families. He would not eat any food until he first gave charity equal to it. Due to his frequent prayer, seven layers of skin would fall from his prostration spots each year. He would collect them, and when he died, they were buried with him.

He wept for his father, al-Husayn (peace be upon him), for twenty years. Whenever food was placed before him, he would weep until a slave said to him: 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, is it not time for your grief to end?' He said: 'Woe to you! The Prophet Jacob (peace be upon him) had twelve sons, and Allah took one from him. His eyes turned white from weeping for him, his head turned gray from sorrow, and his back became hunched from grief, while his son was still alive in the world. I saw my father, my brother, my uncle, and seventeen members of my family killed around me. How can my grief end?'

key_terms.ابْيَضَّتْ عَيْنَاهُ: His eyes turned white (from prolonged weeping/grief)
key_terms.ثَفَنَاتٌ: Layers of skin (peeling from prostration due to frequency)
key_terms.صَلَاةُ مُوَدِّعٍ: A farewell prayer, implying one prays as if it will be their last
key_terms.يَغِيبُونَ فِيهِ: Backbiting him (specifically mentioned in the context of standing before them)

ai.seo_question: What were the key spiritual and social practices of Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin) as described in al-Khisal?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Khisal elucidates the spiritual and social dimensions of Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin), portraying him as the epitome of *khushu'* (humility) in prayer, where physical trembling reflected his awe before the Divine King. It further highlights his dual role as a secret benefactor who bore the weight of charity on his back and a deeply grieving son, linking his personal sorrow to the broader Shia narrative of the Ahl al-Bayt's suffering after Karbala. The text underscores that his worship was not merely ritualistic but a total absorption of the heart, serving as a practical model for the Shia community's devotion and social responsibility.
